basics.name: Kourosh Ghahremani
basics.label: Linguist & Computational Sociolinguistics Researcher
basics.summary: Linguist with a strong theoretical grounding in translation studies, pragmatics, and cross-cultural discourse analysis, now actively developing skills in computational approaches to language. Contributed to peer-reviewed research at EVALITA 2026 on multilingual reclamatory intent detection, where my background in sociolinguistics and translation theory informed cross-lingual feature design and error analysis. Currently building proficiency in Python and machine learning to pursue research at the intersection of linguistic theory and natural language processing.

publications.name: Identity, Toxicity, or Complexity? A Language-Specific Feature Selection Approach to Reclamatory Intent Detection
publications.publisher: Proceedings of EVALITA 2026 (Task A: MultiPRIDE), Bari, Italy
publications.authors: Rajabi, H., Ghavidel, F., & Ghahremani, K.
publications.summary: Multilingual hate-speech detection system (English, Spanish, Italian) combining monolingual BERT embeddings with 61 language-specific sociolinguistic features. Ranked 1st/24 runs on the Italian subtask (Macro F1 = 0.8981). Contribution: cross-lingual sociolinguistic feature framing, design of identity-marker and pragmatic complexity features, and qualitative cross-lingual error analysis.

publications.name: Analysis of Lexical Normalization in the Covid19-related Neologisms: The Case of English to Persian Equivalents
publications.summary: Examined how 29 translators rendered English coroneologisms into Persian; applied Newmark's (1988) normalization taxonomy and Molina & Albir's (2020) translation strategy framework; found that blends and derived words were systematically normalized while old words with new meanings were the least transferable type.

research.name: MultiPRIDE @ EVALITA 2026 — Reclamatory Intent Detection
highlights: Linguistic feature design: Defined and operationalised a framework of 61 sociolinguistic candidate features across three categories — morphosyntactic complexity, sentiment-toxicity dynamics, and identity markers — grounded in pragmatics, sociolinguistics, and translation theory.

Cross-lingual error analysis: Conducted qualitative analysis of 20 misclassified samples per language; identified and named two principal failure modes — the Identity Trap (English agentivity confusion between reclaimer and victim) and Structural Mimicry (Italian genre confusion) — and proposed Semantic Role Labeling as a future architectural remedy.
Multilingual interpretation: Provided the theoretical framing for why reclamation manifests differently per language, drawing on cross-cultural pragmatics and discourse analysis.

Developing computational skills: Engaged with spaCy NLP pipelines, HuggingFace BERT models, and scikit-learn Random Forest as a first entry point into NLP feature extraction and classification workflows.
